label: rem:tjon-universality-external
title: The external three-body/four-body correlation, and why it does not license the simplex baseline
html:
The many-body magnitude leg of \Delta_\lambda is scored against an external observable — the empirical correlation between three-body and four-body binding energies, known in nuclear physics as the Tjon line. The folio carries no statement of what that literature actually establishes, which leaves an analogy free to be read as an established premise. This remark states the external result, states the corpus construction, and separates them.

The external results

Two results are used.

No four-body parameter at leading order. Working in an effective theory of short-range interactions whose two-body scattering length a is large compared with the natural low-energy length scale \ell of the interaction (|a| \gg \ell), Platter, Hammer and Meißner find that an \mathrm{SU}(4)-symmetric one-parameter three-nucleon interaction suffices to renormalise the four-nucleon system at leading order in \ell/|a|; the empirical triton–\alpha correlation then ``follows immediately'', swept out by varying that single three-body parameter [platter2005tjon]. With the binding energies B(^2\mathrm{H}) = 2.22 MeV and B(^3\mathrm{H}) = 8.48 MeV as inputs they obtain a binding energy B(\alpha) \approx 29.5 MeV for the \alpha-particle, against a Coulomb-corrected experimental 29.0 \pm 0.1 MeV.

A dimensionless four-to-three ratio. Solving the four-boson Yakubovsky equations with no four-body parameter at all, Hammer and Platter report that away from threshold the four-body ground state and the deepest three-body state are related by a factor of 5 [hammer2007fourbody]. The correlation is approximately linear away from threshold for either sign of a, with positive curvature for a > 0 and negative curvature for a < 0; the nonlinearity is confined to the threshold region.

Limits of the external results

Each of the following is a separate statement that the results above do not license, and the distinctions matter because the corpus scores against these numbers.

  1. No four-body parameter is needed'' is not no four-body force exists.'' The first is a statement about what a calculation requires for renormalisation; the second is a statement about nature. The four-nucleon force is small, not absent: Jurgenson, Navrátil and Furnstahl measure the similarity-renormalisation-group-induced four-body contribution at ^4\mathrm{He} as a net effect of order tens of keV, with the long-range N^3LO estimate of order a few hundred keV [jurgenson2009srg].

  2. The leading-order claim is contested. Yamashita et al. find a strong sensitivity of the deepest four-body energy to a four-body subtraction constant, and conclude that a four-body parameter should generally enter at leading order. The disagreement is recorded in [hammer2007fourbody] itself, which also notes that Yamashita et al. hold four-body systems of ^4\mathrm{He} atoms and nucleons to be special cases where this sensitivity is absent, repulsive interactions suppressing the probability of four particles being close together. So for the nuclear case both sides agree; for the general case they do not, and [hammer2007fourbody] stresses that its universality rests on the renormalisation-group analysis it inherits.

  3. The zero-range limit is not the nuclear regime. The universal ratio 5 is a zero-range result. Nature, from AME2020 [ame2020], gives B(^4\mathrm{He})/B(^3\mathrm{H}) \approx 3.42 after Coulomb correction. The gap is expected: [platter2005tjon] states that its leading-order Tjon line is shifted from the empirical one precisely because finite-range effects are neglected.

Inequivalence with the simplex condition

The magnitude sidecar expands the many-body binding moment in a simplex (inclusion–exclusion) basis,

  M(A) \;=\; \sum_k \mu_k \binom{A}{k},

in which ``no four-body parameter'' reads as the single condition \mu_4 = 0, equivalent to M(4) = 4M(3) - 6M(2). It is tempting to read the external result as establishing that condition. It does not, and the two are provably inequivalent.

On the \mu_4 = 0 baseline the four-to-three ratio obeys M(4) < 4\,M(3) strictly, for any \mu_2 > 0 and whatever \mu_3 may be — the gap is exactly -6\mu_2. The universal ratio 5 therefore lies outside the baseline's reachable range altogether, so a calculation carrying no four-body input at all can sit at a ratio the simplex condition cannot produce. Conversely, feeding M(4) = 5\,M(3) into the basis returns

  \mu_4 \;=\; 9\mu_2 + \mu_3,

which at the nuclear (\mu_2, \mu_3) is \approx 9.81 — some 2.6 times the value the nuclear data themselves produce. The fourth moment is therefore largest in the calculation that contains no four-body input, which is a direct statement that \mu_4's magnitude is an artifact of the basis rather than a measurement of four-body physics.

There is a blunter way to see the same thing, and it should be stated because the name invites the opposite reading. Three moments are fitted to three anchors (A = 2, 3, 4), so the system is exactly determined and

  \mu_4 \;:=\; M(4) - 4M(3) + 6M(2)

is a definition, carrying zero residual freedom. Writing \mu_4 is therefore another way of writing the amount by which $M(4)$ exceeds the two-point prediction'', and nothing more. It is not a measurement of a four-body interaction, and calling it the four-body moment'' — as the surrounding literature's vocabulary tempts one to — asserts an identification that no step above establishes. The corpus rule this instantiates is defined residual \neq derived decomposition: a residual introduced with := acquires no physical content from the index it is written under.

Both facts are formalised, sorry-free and over a generic commutative ring, in QOU.MassTheory.TjonSimplexForm — tjon_baseline_lt_four_ratio, universal_ratio_not_in_tjon_baseline and universal_ratio_forces_mu4 — and measured in computations/deltalambda/tjon_external_cross_check_probe.py.

The consequence for the magnitude leg is a constraint on citation, not a new result. The external literature may be cited for why a nonzero \mu_4 is worth attending to at all — it registers a real departure of M(4) from the two-point prediction, which is information about the binding curve — and never as a derivation of the simplex form, nor as licence to read that departure as four-body physics.
